beats.intro: Derivatives, module six. [[sub]]Futures are forwards with daily settlement. This chapter shows what that changes, and what it does not.
beats.price: [[a]]A futures contract starts with a value of zero, and its price follows the same no-arbitrage logic as a forward: the spot price, compounded at the risk-free rate. [[ex]]Gold is at seventeen seventy, the rate is two percent, and the contract settles in ninety-one days. [[calc]]The futures price is seventeen seventy-eight seventy-six per ounce, or one hundred seventy-seven thousand eight hundred seventy-six dollars for a hundred ounces. The same as the forward price. [[st]]Add storage and insurance of two dollars at the end, with a present value of one ninety-nine, and the futures price rises to seventeen eighty seventy-six. [[note]]As with forwards, a futures price far below that level may point to a convenience yield.
beats.mtm: [[a]]The difference shows up after inception. Procam holds a forward and a futures contract, both at seventeen seventy-eight seventy-six. [[fwd]]The forward price never changes. Its value is the spot price minus the present value of that price. Seventy-one days in, gold has fallen to seventeen twenty. The value is negative fifty-six eighty-three per ounce, a loss of fifty-six hundred eighty-three dollars on a hundred ounces. It is not settled until maturity. [[fut]]The futures contract settles every day. On day one, the futures price falls five dollars. Procam loses five hundred, and the margin account drops to forty-four fifty, below the maintenance level. [[call]]A margin call of five hundred restores it to forty-nine fifty. [[reset]]And the contract's value resets to zero. [[tab]]After day one, the forward carries an unsettled loss of four ninety-eight, while the futures contract has a value of zero and has paid out five hundred. After day two, the forward's unsettled loss is eight ninety-five, and the futures loss paid that day is four hundred. [[pt]]Cumulatively, the realized gains and losses are about the same. What differs is the timing of the cash, and the credit risk.
beats.irfut: [[a]]Interest rate futures trade on a price, not a rate: one hundred minus the yield. [[ex]]A price of ninety-eight twenty-five means a market reference rate of one point seven five percent. [[dir]]A long position gains when prices rise, which means rates fall. A short position gains when rates rise, just like a fixed-rate payer in a forward rate agreement. [[bpv]]The value of one basis point is the notional, times point zero one percent, times the period. On a million dollars for three months, it is twenty-five dollars. [[bw]]Baywhite funds a loan with one-month floating money, and fears higher rates. It sells futures on fifty million dollars. One basis point is worth four sixteen sixty-seven. [[res]]It sells at ninety-eight seventy-five, and the contract settles at ninety-seven seventy-five. That is a hundred basis points, and a gain of forty-one thousand six hundred sixty-seven dollars.
beats.diff: [[a]]Forward and futures prices are equal under two conditions: interest rates are constant, or they are uncorrelated with futures prices. [[pos]]If futures prices rise along with interest rates, a long futures position is more attractive than a long forward. Profits arrive when rates are high, so they are reinvested at higher rates, and losses arrive when rates are lower. [[neg]]If prices and rates move in opposite directions, the long forward is more attractive. [[rule]]The more attractive contract tends to have the higher price. [[pt]]For short maturities, the differences are usually very small.
beats.convex: [[a]]For interest rates, one difference remains even at short maturities: convexity bias. [[fut]]A futures contract has a fixed value per basis point. Each one is worth exactly twenty-five dollars on this contract. [[fra]]A forward rate agreement settles at the start of the period, so its payment is discounted. [[tab]]With rates at two point two one percent, a fall of ten basis points pays two hundred fifty on the futures, but two forty-eight sixty-nine on the FRA. A rise of ten costs two fifty on the futures, and two forty-eight fifty-six on the FRA. [[pt]]The futures payoff is a straight line. The FRA payoff is not. That curvature is convexity, and it grows with the discounting period.
beats.clearing: [[a]]Central clearing narrows the gap further. [[stress]]Under stress, a futures counterparty that cannot meet a margin call is closed out early, while a flexible OTC forward may stay open. [[ccp]]But dealers must now post margin to a central counterparty, and they usually ask their end users for margin too. [[res]]So forwards increasingly behave like futures, and the cash flow differences between them shrink. [[cost]]Either way, participants need cash or eligible collateral on hand, and must weigh financing, transaction, and administrative costs.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]A futures price equals the forward price: spot compounded at the risk-free rate, adjusted for carry. [[w2]]Futures settle daily and reset to zero. Forwards settle at maturity. Cumulative gains are about equal. [[w3]]Interest rate futures are priced at one hundred minus the yield, with a fixed value per basis point. [[w4]]Correlation and convexity can separate futures from forwards, and central clearing narrows the gap.
